Starting Solids: Baby’s First Foods

Actualizado: July 1, 2026

Este artículo se muestra en inglés mientras se prepara su traducción.

Starting solids is one of the most photographed , and messiest , milestones of the first year. Around six months, most babies are ready to explore food beyond milk. Here is how to spot readiness, what to offer first, and how to keep those early meals safe and low-stress.

Signs your baby is ready

Most babies are ready for solids around six months, but the calendar is only part of the story. Look for the readiness signs: sitting upright with minimal support, good head and neck control, showing real interest in your food, and being able to move food to the back of the mouth and swallow rather than pushing it straight back out with the tongue.

Reaching for food or opening wide when a spoon approaches are good hints. Waking more at night or chewing on hands alone are not reliable signs , those happen for lots of reasons. If you are unsure whether your baby is ready, your pediatrician can help you decide.

Great first foods

There is no single required first food. Iron-rich options are a smart early priority , iron-fortified infant cereal, well-cooked and pureed or shredded meat, beans, and lentils , because babies’ iron stores start to run down around six months.

From there, variety is the goal: soft fruits like banana, pear, and cooked apple, vegetables like sweet potato and avocado, plus grains and dairy such as plain yogurt. Offering many flavors and textures early, including bitter vegetables, helps shape adventurous tastes later.

Milk , breast milk or formula , remains the main source of nutrition for most of the first year. Early solids are about practice and exposure as much as calories.

Purees, baby-led weaning, or both?

Traditional weaning starts with smooth purees and gradually thickens textures. Baby-led weaning skips purees and offers soft, graspable finger foods , think steamed broccoli florets or strips of avocado , letting the baby feed themselves from the start.

Research has not crowned a winner, and many families happily mix both: purees at some meals, soft finger foods at others. Whichever route you choose, progress textures steadily , babies who stay on smooth purees too long can become reluctant to accept lumps.

The non-negotiables are the same either way: baby sits upright in a high chair, an adult supervises every bite, and food is soft enough to squish between your fingers.

Introducing allergens

Current guidance has flipped from the old advice to delay allergens. Introducing common allergy foods , peanut (as smooth peanut butter thinned into puree, never whole nuts), egg, dairy, wheat, soy, fish, and sesame , early and regularly, from around six months, appears to reduce the risk of food allergies.

Introduce one new allergen at a time, in a small amount, earlier in the day so you can watch for reactions like hives, vomiting, or unusual fussiness. If your baby has severe eczema or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before starting allergens , they may recommend a tailored plan.

Foods to avoid in the first year

A few firm rules: no honey before the first birthday, because of the risk of infant botulism , this includes baked goods made with honey. No cow’s milk as the main drink before one year (small amounts in cooking or yogurt and cheese are fine).

Skip choking hazards: whole nuts, whole grapes (quarter them lengthwise), popcorn, hard raw vegetables, chunks of nut butter, hot dogs cut into coins, and hard candies. Also avoid added salt and sugar where you can, and low-calorie or highly caffeinated drinks entirely.

It is worth learning the difference between gagging and choking. Gagging is noisy, common, and part of learning to eat; choking is silent. Many parents feel calmer after taking an infant first-aid course.

Mess is part of the process

Squished banana in the hair and yogurt on the floor are not failures , they are how babies learn about texture, temperature, and self-feeding. Exploration with hands is genuinely valuable, so let it happen as much as your patience allows.

Keep portions tiny, expect plenty of food to end up anywhere but the mouth, and remember that appetite varies wildly from day to day. Your job is to offer good food in a relaxed setting; your baby’s job is to decide how much to eat.

Puntos clave

  • Start solids around 6 months, when baby sits well, holds their head steady, and shows interest in food.
  • Prioritize iron-rich first foods, then build variety in flavors and textures.
  • Purees and baby-led weaning both work , many families mix the two.
  • Introduce common allergens early and one at a time; ask your doctor first if baby has severe eczema.
  • No honey before age one, and always avoid choking hazards like whole grapes and nuts.

Preguntas frecuentes

How much should my baby actually eat at first?

Very little , a teaspoon or two is a fine start. Early solids are about practice and exposure; breast milk or formula still provides most nutrition for months. Let your baby’s interest guide the amount.

Why is honey off-limits before age one?

Honey can contain spores that cause infant botulism, a rare but serious illness in babies under one. This applies to raw and cooked honey, including baked goods. After the first birthday it is considered safe.

What if my baby gags on lumpy food?

Occasional gagging is a normal protective reflex while babies learn to manage textures , it is noisy and usually resolves on its own. Choking, by contrast, is silent and needs immediate action. Keep pieces soft and appropriately sized, always supervise, and consider an infant first-aid course for confidence.
